title: Planning, reviews, retrospectives and workshops
blurb: Explain the purpose of planning, stand-ups, reviews and demos, retrospectives and facilitated workshops, and who takes part in each.
question: At the end of an iteration, a team shows new features to site managers and then, separately, discusses how to work better next time. Which two agile events are these, and how do they differ?

teach.h: Regular events keep feedback loops short
teach.body: Planning, review and retrospectives are recurring agile events. PRINCE2 Agile runs many of them as workshops: facilitated, collaborative sessions with a defined purpose, participants, agenda topics and outputs. Version 2 attaches named workshops to every process. Because change and uncertainty are high, feedback loops are small and frequent, and reporting is often handled informally through these workshops and visually through burn charts and dashboards.

teach.caption: Plan, build, show, improve, then plan again.

Purpose
Who takes part
rows: Prepare the next iteration; team plan
Delivery team and PO; team coach facilitates
Short daily check on progress and obstacles
Delivery team; PM by the team's agreement

teach.caption: The team coach facilitates team workshops (Table B.1). Scrum's equivalent of the stand-up is the Daily Scrum.

teach.body: The team planning workshop, in managing product delivery, prepares the next iteration. Its topics are product backlog refinement (MoSCoW), user story refinement, effort estimation and iteration planning, giving a realistic team plan. Detailed task planning is done only for the next iteration. At stage boundaries, the release planning workshop (introduction, OKR definition, release planning, wrap-up) updates the release map for the next stage.

The progress review workshop, in controlling a stage, assesses status, celebrates achievements and tackles challenges using metrics, accomplishments and open risks. Its product demo topic shows completed features to showcase progress and gather user acceptance and feedback, while project highlights reviews the project dashboard. Evaluating stage status happens in a progress review, and demos also support organizational change by engaging users and speeding adoption.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 13.5.4.1, Tables 13.9 and 13.10, 4.2.4

teach.body: The team retrospective takes place at the end of each iteration, not during it, so it is not a way to track progress. Its topics are the good, the bad, the learning and team building. Risks are also identified in every planning session and retrospective. The daily stand-up keeps work visible to the whole team; the project manager may attend only with the delivery team's agreement.

Team coach Siobhan Kelly facilitates the site safety app team's planning workshop each fortnight. Project manager Daniel Osei asks to join the daily stand-ups; the team agrees he can attend on Fridays. At the progress review, site managers try the near-miss reporting form in the product demo and ask for photo upload. In the retrospective, the team celebrates fast feedback, notes late test devices, agrees to book devices earlier and ends with a team lunch.

teach.text: The review and demo looks at the PRODUCT (what was built, with users); the retrospective looks at the TEAM'S WAY OF WORKING (how to improve). Retrospectives come at the end of an iteration, not as a progress check during it. And the project manager joins stand-ups by the team's agreement, not by right.

items: Workshop: facilitated session with defined purpose, participants, agenda topics and outputs (5.6.3.1).
Team planning: next iteration; refinement, estimation, iteration planning; team plan.
Release planning: stage boundary; OKRs and the release map.
Progress review: dashboard metrics, risks and a product demo for user feedback.
Retrospective: end of iteration; the good, the bad, the learning, team building.
Stand-up: daily team sync; the PM attends with the team's agreement.

summary: You can now explain the purpose of team planning, stand-ups, reviews and demos, retrospectives and other workshops, and who takes part in each. You can also tell a product demo from a retrospective and team planning from release planning.

A.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, what is a workshop?
options: A training course the agile coach runs for new teams
A facilitated session with set purpose, agenda and outputs
A formal board meeting that approves each stage plan
An informal catch-up between the PM and a product owner
A.why: A workshop is a facilitated, collaborative session with a defined purpose, participants, agenda topics and outputs (5.6.3.1).

whyNot.0: Training is part of building agile maturity; a workshop is a working session with set outputs.
whyNot.2: Stage authorization is a directing decision; workshops are collaborative working sessions.
whyNot.3: An informal catch-up has no defined agenda or outputs.

A.q: When does a team retrospective take place?
options: At the end of each iteration
At the start of each iteration
Daily, before work begins
Once, at project closure
A.why: The team retrospective workshop reflects on the last iteration, so it happens at the end of each iteration (13.6.4.2).

whyNot.1: The start of an iteration is for team planning.
whyNot.2: A daily check-in is the stand-up, not a retrospective.
whyNot.3: Project-level lessons are gathered at closure, but team retrospectives happen every iteration.

A.q: Which topic of the progress review workshop shows completed features to gather user acceptance and feedback?
options: Welcome
Project highlights
Product demo
Current risks and issues
A.why: The product demo shows completed features to showcase progress and gather user acceptance and feedback (Table 13.10).

whyNot.0: The welcome sets the scene, agenda and goals and introduces those taking part.
whyNot.1: Project highlights reviews metrics and accomplishments on the project dashboard.
whyNot.3: Current risks and issues discusses open risks and issues, not product features.

B.q: The project manager wants to attend the delivery team's daily stand-ups. What does PRINCE2 Agile say?
options: The PM must attend every stand-up to report upwards
The PM may attend if the board has approved it
The PM should send project support instead
The PM may attend with the delivery team's agreement
B.why: Table 12.1: the project manager may attend daily stand-ups with the delivery team's agreement.

whyNot.0: Stand-ups belong to the delivery team; the PM pulls progress from the team dashboard.
whyNot.1: The decision rests with the delivery team, not the board.
whyNot.2: Project support pulls information from dashboards; it is not a stand-in at stand-ups.

B.q: What is the purpose of the team planning workshop?
options: To prepare for the next iteration and produce a team plan
To update the release map and OKRs for the next stage
To reflect on what went well in the last iteration
To show completed features to users for feedback
B.why: The team planning workshop prepares the next iteration, ending with iteration planning and a realistic team plan (13.6.4.1).

whyNot.1: Updating the release map and OKRs is the release planning workshop at a stage boundary.
whyNot.2: Reflecting on the last iteration is the team retrospective.
whyNot.3: Showing features to users is the product demo in the progress review workshop.

B.q:
Which two statements about agile events in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. Retrospectives are a fixed point for identifying risks.
2. Retrospectives are used to track progress during an iteration.
3. The agile enablement workshop is for the project board, agile coaches and business representatives.
4. The product demo is a topic of the team retrospective workshop.
options: 1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
2 and 4
B.why: Risk identification is a fixed part of every planning session and retrospective (10.3.1), and the agile enablement workshop is for the board, agile coaches and business representatives (13.3.3).

whyNot.1: Statement 4 is wrong: the product demo is a topic of the progress review workshop.
whyNot.2: Statement 2 is wrong: retrospectives happen at the end of an iteration, not to track progress during it.
whyNot.3: Both are wrong: retrospectives come at the end of an iteration rather than tracking progress during it, and the product demo belongs to the progress review workshop.

C.q: Under which topic of the team retrospective would a team record the action 'book test devices a week before each iteration'?
options: The good
The bad
The learning
Team building
C.why: The learning captures lessons, improvement suggestions and actionable insights (Table 13.14).

whyNot.0: The good celebrates what went well.
whyNot.1: The bad identifies issues and their causes; the agreed improvement belongs under the learning.
whyNot.3: Team building strengthens bonds, for example with a game or food.

C.q: Which workshop updates the release map and team OKRs, and in which process is it held?
options: Team planning workshop; managing product delivery
Release planning workshop; managing a stage boundary
Progress review workshop; controlling a stage
Project kickoff workshop; initiating a project
C.why: The release planning workshop, in managing a stage boundary, covers OKR definition and release planning to update the release map (13.7.4.1).

whyNot.0: Team planning prepares the next iteration and produces a team plan.
whyNot.2: The progress review assesses status and demos the product; it does not set OKRs.
whyNot.3: The kickoff workshop builds teamwork, values, matrices and dashboards.

C.q: Which is NOT a topic of the team planning workshop?
options: Product backlog refinement
Effort estimation
Iteration planning
The learning
C.why: 'The learning' is a topic of the team retrospective, not the team planning workshop (Tables 13.13 and 13.14).

whyNot.0: Product backlog refinement is a team planning topic.
whyNot.1: Effort estimation is a team planning topic.
whyNot.2: Iteration planning is a team planning topic.

reteach.title: A football squad's week
reteach.question: How does a football squad's week of team talk, training, match and debrief map onto agile events?

blocks.body: Before the week, the squad plans what to work on: team planning. Each morning a quick huddle checks who is fit and what is blocking anyone: the stand-up. The match shows the fans what the team can do: the review and demo. Afterwards, the debrief asks how to play better next time: the retrospective.

blocks.text: The match (demo) is about the result users see; the debrief (retrospective) is about how the team works.

explain.body: A workshop is a facilitated session with a defined purpose, participants, agenda topics and outputs. Every process has named workshops, for example the agile enablement workshop in directing a project, where the board and agile coaches regularly reassess the Agilometer.

test.q: Which workshop belongs to the directing a project process and regularly reassesses the Agilometer?
options: Agile enablement workshop
Project initiation workshop
Progress review workshop
Team retrospective workshop
test.why: The agile enablement workshop, in directing a project, holds regular Agilometer assessments for the board, agile coaches and business representatives (Table 13.5).

whyNot.1: The project initiation workshop first assesses the Agilometer, but it belongs to initiating a project.
whyNot.2: The progress review workshop is in controlling a stage.
whyNot.3: The team retrospective is in managing product delivery.

explain.body: The team planning workshop prepares the next iteration: refine the backlog and stories, estimate effort, then plan the iteration. Task-level planning is done for the next iteration only; stage boundaries update the release map.

test.q: Detailed, task-level planning is done for which horizon?
options: The whole project
The current stage
The next iteration
The next release
test.why: Plans are made just in time: task-level planning happens for the next iteration in managing product delivery.

whyNot.0: The whole project is planned at a high level on the release map.
whyNot.1: The stage is planned as an updated release map, not at task level.
whyNot.3: Releases are planned at feature level on the release map.

explain.body: In the progress review workshop, the product demo shows completed features so users can give acceptance and feedback, and project highlights reviews the project dashboard.

test.q: What is the main aim of a product demo?
options: To agree the team's improvement actions
To showcase progress and gather user feedback
To re-estimate the remaining backlog items
To approve the plan for the next stage
test.why: The product demo showcases progress and gathers user acceptance and feedback (Table 13.10).

whyNot.0: Improvement actions come from the retrospective's 'the learning' topic.
whyNot.2: Re-estimating is effort estimation in team planning.
whyNot.3: Approving the next stage plan is a board decision in directing a project.

explain.body: The retrospective, at the end of each iteration, looks at how the team works: the good, the bad, the learning, team building. The daily stand-up keeps work visible; the PM attends with the team's agreement.

test.q: A team's retrospective MAINLY looks at:
options: the features users accepted in the demo
the board's tolerances for the current stage
the cost of the iteration so far against budget
how the team can improve its way of working
test.why: A retrospective reflects on the last iteration to learn lessons and improve the team's way of working (13.6.4.2).

whyNot.0: Feature acceptance happens in the product demo.
whyNot.1: Tolerances are set by the board, not reviewed in team retrospectives.
whyNot.2: Cost has zero tolerance; the retrospective focuses on ways of working.
